flawed_step: The claim that being triangle-free with Delta<=4 forces chromatic number <=3 is false. The Chvátal graph is triangle-free and 4-regular, and its chromatic number is 4.
counterexample:
The Chvátal graph has vertices 0..11. Its adjacency lists are: 0:{1,4,6,9}, 1:{0,2,5,7}, 2:{1,3,6,8}, 3:{2,4,7,9}, 4:{0,3,5,8}, 5:{1,4,10,11}, 6:{0,2,10,11}, 7:{1,3,8,11}, 8:{2,4,7,10}, 9:{0,3,10,11}, 10:{5,6,8,9}, 11:{5,6,7,9}. That gives 24 edges, and every vertex has degree 4.

Triangle-free: I checked all 24 edges, and in each case the two endpoints have no common neighbour.

Not 3-colourable: note that 0-1-2-3-4-0 is a 5-cycle. Suppose there is a proper colouring with colours a, b, c. Vertices 10 and 11 are not adjacent, and their common neighbours are 5, 6 and 9.

Case B: c(10)=a and c(11)=b. Then 5, 6 and 9 must all be c. Each of vertices 0 to 4 is adjacent to one of 5, 6 or 9, so each of them avoids c. That would 2-colour the 5-cycle, which is impossible.

Case A: c(10)=c(11)=a. Then 5 to 9 all avoid a. Among 5 to 9 the only edge is 7-8, so we may name the colours so that 7=b and 8=c.
- If 5=b: then 4=a.
  - If 6=b: then 2=a and 3=c, which forces 9=b and 0=c. Now 1 is adjacent to 0(c), 2(a) and 7(b), so it has no colour.
  - If 6=c and 9=b: then 0=a, but 0 is adjacent to 4=a.
  - If 6=c and 9=c: then 0=b, so 3 must be a, but 3 is adjacent to 4=a.
- If 5=c: then 1=a.
  - If 6=b: then 2=a, but 2 is adjacent to 1=a.
  - If 6=c: then 2=b.
    - If 9=b: then 0=a, but 0 is adjacent to 1=a.
    - If 9=c: then 3=a and 0=b. Now 4 is adjacent to 0(b), 3(a) and 8(c), so it has no colour.

Every case leads to a contradiction, so the chromatic number is 4.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. The Chvátal graph (12 vertices, given by explicit adjacency lists) is a simple, triangle-free graph in which every vertex has degree 4, so it meets the hypothesis under either reading of "maximum degree 4". A complete case analysis on the colours of vertices 10 and 11 shows it has no proper 3-colouring.
